Heather Sharpes-Smith, Executive Director of URI Online, JCODL Chair Purpose of the Committee The purpose of the Joint Committee on Online and Distance Learning (JCODL) is to propose, examine, and recommend institutional policies and practices for developing, planning, and evaluating online and distance learning with a focus on quality, sustainability, and connection to the University’s mission, with approval of the Faculty Senate and Provost.
Further, JCODL considers faculty training, quality in delivery of online offerings, student learning outcomes, and ADA compliance regarding online and distance learning, as well as develops and implements strategic plans for online courses, certificate, and degree programs. (University Manual 5.78.10 - 5.78.11).
Executive Summary The committee discussed several topics internally (listed in the next section) during the 2025-2026 academic year.
The committee did not bring forward any proposals for consideration and a vote to the university’s Faculty Senate.
However, the Faculty Senate did discuss a new structure for the committee during the spring 2026 semester.

As of the April 2026 Faculty Senate meeting, no changes had been made to the committee’s structure.
Internal Topics of Discussion During the 2025-2026 Academic Year Fall 2025 With the addition of new members added to the committee this year, the fall semester served as a regrounding and educational opportunity to ensure that all of the members of the committee were aware of the current structure and professional development opportunities available to

faculty who want to teach online at URI.
During this semester, Joannah Portman-Daley, Director of URI Online’s Online Education & Instructional Design team, led presentations to ensure that all members of the committee were aware of current opportunities related to online learning professional development that are available on the campus including the list of qualified instructors and the 4 current pathways for becoming qualified to teach online .
Spring 2026 At the start of the spring 2026 semester, Chris Lavan resigned as chair of the committee and moved to the role of Provost Office’s designee.
This was done for 2 reasons.
First, to fully recognize URI Online as the unit holding the university’s expertise for online learning and instructional design.
Second, to provide the committee with the leadership it needed to properly engage in the current strategic needs of the university related to online learning.
Subsequently, Heather Sharpes-Smith became the chair of the committee during this semester.
The spring semester also included continued discussion of the upcoming alignment and merging of accelerated and traditional academic calendars and the broader implications for online learning.

The committee discussed how this transition affects online course scheduling, student registration patterns, faculty planning, instructional design timelines, student support, and operational coordination across academic and administrative units.
These conversations also reinforced URI Online’s expanded scope, with all online programs — whether 14-week traditional online offerings or 7-week accelerated offerings — falling under URIO’s purview.
This alignment is intended to support clearer governance, more coordinated planning, consistency in the online student experience, and stronger institutional oversight of online learning across the university.

The spring semester also included: ● Information about the proposed Brightspace Change process led by Michelle Rogers, Director of Teaching & Learning Services. ● Information about the new program process led by Joannah Portman-Daley to ensure that all members of the committee were aware of the forthcoming process that academic departments and colleges must complete to propose a new academic program online. ● Information about training opportunity to support faculty in making courses in Brightspace more accessible, led by Michelle Rogers. ● Multi-factor authentication being turned on in Engage, the university’s LMS for non-degree related educational opportunities, by Michelle Rogers. ● Awareness of the renewal of the university’s NC-Sara members by committee chair and URI Online Executive Director, Heather Sharpes-Smith. ● Information about ADA compliance procedures and digital course content, as well as an overview of the Provost Office’s faculty resource site in Brightspace led by Heather Sharpes-Smith and Joannah Portman-Daley ● Information about the university’s “Digital Accessibility: Understanding Your Rights and Responsibilities” event on March 30, 2026, including URI’s new digital accessibility webpage , led by Heather.

PROGRAM REPORT Special Summer Curriculum Committee Report 2026-2027-SSCC-02-B At the July 14, 2026 meeting of the Special Summer Curriculum Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate Executive Committee for approval. for confirmation by the senate PROGRAM MODIFICATIONS Communicative Disorders - Minor, Spring 2027 Appendix A Change description, course requirements NEW MINOR Ocean Innovation - Minor, Spring 2027 Appendix B The minor in Ocean Innovation is designed for students who want to apply innovation and problem-solving skills in ocean-based contexts and industries. The minor is intended for students pursuing majors across the University who are interested in creating new ventures, innovating within established organizations, or contributing to interdisciplinary teams addressing challenges and opportunities connected to the ocean, coasts, and related systems. Students completing the minor develop skills to identify and evaluate opportunities, apply innovative thinking to complex systems, and translate scientific, technical, and environmental knowledge into viable solutions. The minor emphasizes innovation in areas such as ocean and coastal industries, food and energy systems, climate and resilience, data-driven decision-making, and sustainability-focused business models. In addition to fulfilling all the basic requirements for a minor (see Minor Fields of Study), students declaring an Ocean Innovation minor must complete 18 credits. The College of Business administers the Ocean Innovation minor in collaboration with academic units across the University. Interested students should contact their academic advisor for further information.

The primary goal of the BS in Interdisciplinary Applied Artificial Intelligence is to prepare graduates who can apply artificial intelligence responsibly, creatively, and effectively across domains, integrating technical skills with ethical reasoning, interdisciplinary collaboration, and real-world problem solving.
The program emphasizes applied and lifelong learning, workforce relevance, and societal impact, ensuring that graduates are prepared for both immediate employment and long- term career adaptability.
It advances student success, retention, timely degree completion, and career readiness.
The program’s applied focus, interdisciplinary design, and integration of experiential learning opportunities support students in developing market- relevant skills that align with workforce needs.
By embedding internships, project-based learning, and applied AI coursework throughout the curriculum, the program enhances students’ engagement, persistence, and post-graduation outcomes while positioning URI graduates to succeed in a rapidly evolving, AI-enabled economy.

The vision is to provide students with deep knowledge of AI systems and expertise in transferring and applying AI to a variety of problem types.
This program will cover knowledge of the AI ecosystem including the ability to work in interdisciplinary teams with data and domain experts to collect, clean organize, and sample data, match the problem and data to the right intelligent computational tool (there are many types of AI, each with its strengths and weaknesses), tailor, build on top of, and adapt these tools to the problems at hand, support the safe, secure, ethical and accurate reporting of the results to domain experts, and guide teams in deciding if the analytical results make sense.
Students will learn how to use, tailor and augment AI so that the AI can serve as assistants in problem solving, with the human as the master, well versed in the interpretation, and ethical and societal implications of the use of the powerful AI that they will wield.
All of this is in the context of a world in which educators and potential employers are concerned with the lack of digital skills among today’s students and graduates.

To be well educated and prepared for the modern workplace, students must learn to acquire applied technology skills and also to transfer these technologies to specific problems as they arise.
Thus this program is not intended to train students to develop new AI, but to become experts in mastering, adapting, building upon, and deploying existing and evolving intelligent computational artifacts.
We will help students to master the AI tools of today but also help them to understand that these are only contemporary examples to sharpen their problem solving, and learning skills, and give them a leg up as they enter the workplace.
As the world changes and embraces new technologies such as digital twins, and quantum computing, both already inextricably intertwined with AI, we propose a major that is flexible enough that it can evolve with emerging intelligent technologies.
The program advances the University’s goals by preparing students to address complex real-world challenges through the responsible and creative application of emerging technologies.

The curriculum integrates applied coursework, project-based learning, and internships, ensuring that students develop both technical expertise and transferable skills that support career readiness and lifelong learning.
The program reflects the University’s commitment to interdisciplinary problem-solving and collaboration across colleges and departments.
The program also contributes to the University’s role in supporting economic development, innovation, and the future of work in Rhode Island and beyond.
